frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over gas production and export infrastructure, but European demand and price shifts expose fiscal and strategic vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya pressures Algeria's borders and complicates its effort to preserve non-interventionist security influence.

frictionVectors.title: External finance exposure
frictionVectors.details: Angola is reducing dependence on oil-backed Chinese finance, but debt service, foreign operators, and hydrocarbons investment still constrain sovereign economic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Western and Chinese interest in the Lobito rail route is expanding infrastructure options while increasing pressure over access to regional copper and cobalt supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border disruption
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger have threatened trade flows through the Port of Cotonou, exposing Benin's logistics model to regional political decisions beyond its control.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal jihadist spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity moving south from the Sahel is forcing greater reliance on foreign security cooperation and raising costs for northern infrastructure and commerce.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened its negotiating position with De Beers, but diamond marketing, technology, and market access remain partly dependent on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral diversification race
frictionVectors.details: New interest in copper, lithium, and other minerals could broaden sovereign revenues, although foreign capital and infrastructure capacity will shape who captures the value.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal gold insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The state is seeking tighter control over gold production and exports, but insurgent taxation, informal networks, and weak oversight continue to drain resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The junta's expanded security relationship with Russia reduces reliance on Western partners but creates new concerns over accountability, operational dependence, and access to strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Rare-Earth Governance
frictionVectors.details: Informal mining, opaque licensing, and cross-border smuggling limit state capture of mineral value. Foreign traders and regional networks retain significant influence over supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Great Lakes Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained amid competing accusations over armed groups and border insecurity. Instability in eastern DRC continues to absorb Burundi's security resources and complicate trade access.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Connectivity Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its Atlantic position for ports, logistics, and digital connectivity while balancing European, Chinese, and other external financing interests. Debt sustainability and strategic infrastructure ownership remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Resource Enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Illegal fishing and narcotics trafficking challenge control over the country's extensive maritime zone. Limited naval and coast-guard capacity leaves enforcement dependent on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, ports, and major projects deepen infrastructure capacity but increase exposure to external contractors and financing terms. The Kribi corridor remains strategically important for national and regional trade.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Regions and Resource Access
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest continues to disrupt transport, agriculture, and local economic control. Armed groups, security forces, and political elites compete over taxation, territory, and access to natural resources.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian security personnel and associated commercial networks has strengthened regime protection while raising concerns over opaque access to gold and diamond concessions. This limits transparency and bargaining power over national resources.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Trade Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks retain influence over peripheral roads, borderlands, and artisanal mining zones. Weak state logistics and limited infrastructure prevent Bangui from consistently enforcing national resource rules.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon income remains central to state financing, but production and export logistics depend on external operators and the Cameroon pipeline corridor. Revenue concentration leaves sovereignty vulnerable to price shocks and contract asymmetries.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Border and External Security Ties
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war is driving refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border militia risks, especially in eastern Chad. N'Djamena must balance domestic consolidation with security cooperation involving regional and extra-regional partners.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to claim Mayotte, while France maintains administrative control and security ties there. The dispute constrains bilateral relations and complicates migration management.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic fiscal capacity leaves ports, energy, and connectivity projects dependent on external donors and partners, reducing national leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS AND SUPPLY-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains highly exposed to foreign capital, smuggling, and opaque contracting. Kinshasa is seeking greater value capture and diversification, but enforcement and processing capacity remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN SECURITY AND REGIONAL INTERFERENCE
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups continues to undermine state authority and transport corridors. Regional military and political involvement complicates efforts to secure mining zones and border trade.

frictionVectors.title: OIL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues dominate fiscal and export capacity, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price cycles, offshore investment terms, and external energy demand.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT AND STRATEGIC INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction involvement remain important in roads, public works, and resource-linked infrastructure. Debt exposure and limited transparency can constrain independent policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN CAPITAL IN STRATEGIC SECTORS
frictionVectors.details: Ports, energy, telecommunications, and mining remain deeply integrated with multinational firms. Abidjan is gaining bargaining power, but domestic value capture and ownership remain uneven.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA DEPENDENCE AND FARMER INCOMES
frictionVectors.details: Côte d’Ivoire retains major influence as a producer but remains exposed to foreign processing, pricing, and sustainability requirements. Efforts to expand local processing have improved leverage without eliminating vulnerability.

highlights: Bases and ports secure strategic rents
Red Sea tensions raise leverage and risk

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN BASE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences generate revenue and diplomatic weight but limit Djibouti’s room for strategic neutrality. Regional crises increase the value of the base network while raising retaliation risks.

frictionVectors.title: PORTS, DEBT, AND CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti’s ports and rail links are essential to Ethiopia’s trade and remain closely tied to external operators and lenders. The state captures significant rents, but debt exposure and infrastructure dependence constrain sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile allocation
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flow management and seeks a binding operating agreement. The dispute remains intertwined with Sudanese instability and wider Red Sea security.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF support, Gulf investment, and Western financial backing help stabilize Egypt but increase outside leverage over exchange-rate, privatization, and infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling hydrocarbon output narrows fiscal space and increases reliance on foreign operators, technical partners, and regional gas-processing arrangements. Resource nationalism remains strong, but bargaining power is weakening.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Large state-led infrastructure projects remain exposed to Chinese financing, contractor dependence, and weak public transparency. Debt and declining energy revenues constrain sovereign control over future development.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to the Bab el-Mandeb attract attention from Gulf states, Turkey, Egypt, and other security actors. Asmara seeks to monetize access while resisting formal dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide revenue but depend heavily on foreign capital, operators, and export channels. Limited transparency and sanctions risk complicate long-term sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Regional economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African trade, logistics, electricity, and customs systems, limiting room for independent resource and industrial policy.

frictionVectors.title: Market-access vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, textiles, and light manufacturing remain sensitive to external trade preferences and regional supply chains. Shifts in South African or US trade policy could quickly affect employment and foreign exchange.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and GERD confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's energy and diplomatic leverage, but Egypt and Sudan continue to demand binding rules on filling and drought-period operations. The issue remains a major regional escalation risk.

frictionVectors.title: Debt restructuring and telecom opening
frictionVectors.details: Debt relief negotiations and foreign participation in telecommunications and infrastructure provide capital but create policy leverage for creditors and investors. Conflict-related damage and fiscal pressure further limit Addis Ababa's room to maneuver.

highlights: Junta Reasserts Control Over Strategic Assets
Manganese and Oil Drive Resource Nationalism

frictionVectors.title: French Influence and Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater control over oil, mining, and infrastructure arrangements historically linked to French commercial interests. This improves bargaining power but risks investor hesitation and diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou-Style Rail and Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is attempting to expand mineral logistics and domestic processing while relying on foreign capital and contractors. Infrastructure financing could limit practical sovereignty over strategic export corridors.

highlights: Port and Cashew Dependence Constrain Autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Cross-Border Dependence on Senegal
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia depends heavily on Senegal for regional transport, food access, and security cooperation. This stabilizes the country but leaves its strategic autonomy vulnerable to bilateral disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Trade Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port modernization and commercial logistics rely substantially on external financiers and operators. The resulting connectivity gains may not translate into stronger domestic control over trade revenues.

highlights: Gold and Lithium Policy Turns More Assertive

frictionVectors.title: IMF Conditionality and Creditor Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stabilization remains tied to IMF programs, debt restructuring, and external creditor confidence. These constraints narrow policy space even as Ghana works to restore macroeconomic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Critical-Mineral Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining is damaging water systems and challenging state authority, while lithium development raises concerns over export dependence and insufficient domestic processing. Accra is pushing for stronger local-content and value-addition rules.

highlights: Junta Balances China, Gulf, and Western Interests

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Simandou Logistics
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore project is financed and operated through complex foreign-led consortia involving Chinese and other international partners. Rail, port, and processing arrangements could generate growth while preserving external dominance over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Military Rule and Resource Credibility
frictionVectors.details: The junta uses mining negotiations to strengthen domestic legitimacy but faces international pressure over delayed democratic transition. Political uncertainty increases the risk that resource contracts become instruments of elite and foreign leverage.

highlights: Cashew and Cocaine Routes Undermine State Control

frictionVectors.title: Narcotics Transit and Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime enforcement leave Guinea-Bissau exposed to transnational cocaine networks. International security assistance is necessary but can reinforce dependence and fragment sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Export Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy relies heavily on raw cashew exports, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign buyers, price swings, and informal trade channels. Limited processing capacity prevents the country from capturing more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: High debt-service costs limit Nairobi's room to negotiate infrastructure and energy deals with China, Gulf investors, and Western lenders. Pressure is strongest around transport corridors, ports, and public-private concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and transport corridor remain exposed to militant violence, local land disputes, and competition over access to regional trade routes. Instability could weaken Kenya's ability to convert infrastructure into sovereign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Water Export Asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water relationship with South Africa provides vital revenue but leaves Maseru dependent on a larger neighbor for project financing, energy, and market access. Delays and cost disputes can reduce national bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond and Energy Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Diamond exports and hydropower remain exposed to external capital, volatile prices, and South African grid conditions. Limited fiscal capacity restricts Lesotho's ability to capture more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Liberia relies heavily on foreign mining companies and external logistics finance to monetize iron ore. Concession terms, local-content enforcement, and port access remain central tests of whether the state captures durable value.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors and development partners compete for influence over ports, roads, energy, and telecommunications. Weak domestic financing leaves Monrovia vulnerable to unfavorable long-term infrastructure arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Facilities and Revenue Control
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and armed networks can disrupt production, exports, and budget transfers through control of fields, pipelines, terminals, or the central financial system. Hydrocarbon wealth remains a source of factional leverage rather than unified national power.

frictionVectors.title: External Military Patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Egypt, the UAE, and European actors retain influence through security partnerships, arms, diplomacy, or migration arrangements. Their involvement constrains Libya's ability to establish an independent security architecture and coherent resource policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, ilmenite, and other mineral projects depend heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Madagascar faces persistent pressure to prioritize investment flows over stronger domestic processing and revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Limited port, power, and transport capacity increases reliance on overseas operators and financiers. Maritime insecurity, illegal fishing, and weak enforcement further erode control over surrounding economic waters.

highlights: Energy and fertilizer security remain exposed

frictionVectors.title: External debt and reform conditionality
frictionVectors.details: IMF-led stabilization and creditor negotiations limit Malawi's fiscal autonomy and shape decisions on subsidies, public investment, and state-owned enterprises.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic minerals and power deficits
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in mining is expanding while unreliable electricity and imported fuel reduce the state's ability to capture value from emerging mineral projects.

highlights: Junta tightens control over strategic mining

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Disputes with major foreign mining operators reflect Bamako's effort to raise state revenues and renegotiate contracts, but they risk investment disruption and arbitration.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security support has increased political room for the junta while narrowing relations with Western partners and complicating access to finance and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas governance
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major revenue and diplomatic benefits, but cross-border production, local-content, and revenue-sharing arrangements remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of logistics
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate mining, ports, and prospective hydrogen infrastructure, creating potential gaps between export growth and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Indian Ocean alignment
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to balance sovereignty claims and security cooperation involving the Chagos Archipelago, India, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

frictionVectors.title: Port and undersea-infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Competition among external partners for maritime logistics, connectivity, and digital infrastructure creates strategic opportunities but requires careful neutrality management.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Control and development of the territory strengthen Morocco's economic position, but legal challenges and diplomatic opposition continue to affect foreign investment and trade.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in energy and industry
frictionVectors.details: European investment in renewables, automotive supply chains, and energy interconnections supports industrial sovereignty while leaving Morocco exposed to foreign technology, finance, and market demand.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks continue to threaten LNG-linked infrastructure and local communities. Reliance on foreign security support limits Maputo's autonomous control over the gas corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and lenders retain major influence over project timing, financing, and revenue structures. Domestic value capture remains constrained by security and infrastructure gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Governance
frictionVectors.details: Recent oil discoveries have attracted major foreign operators, creating pressure for stronger local-content rules and transparent revenue management. Namibia retains policy space but faces capacity and bargaining challenges.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Ports, water, electricity, and transport links may constrain the scale-up of offshore oil and green-hydrogen projects. External capital remains central to closing these gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence continues to threaten mining zones, roads, and energy infrastructure. Security partnerships are shifting away from Western actors, but alternative support has not eliminated operational risk.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Uranium Access
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater control over uranium and petroleum assets while relations with foreign operators remain tense. Pipeline and border-access disputes could sharply limit export revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism, and insecurity continue to reduce state and community returns from petroleum production. Weak enforcement and opaque contracting undermine sovereign resource control.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Refinery, gas, and power expansion relies heavily on foreign finance, technology, and private operators. The Dangote refinery improves strategic autonomy but does not resolve broader grid and logistics weaknesses.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Accusations over support for armed groups and mineral flows from eastern Congo expose Rwanda to diplomatic pressure and potential sanctions. Regional instability threatens trade access and the legitimacy of its mineral strategy.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security influence exceeds its economic weight, but it remains dependent on foreign markets, aid, and investment. This creates leverage for outside actors despite strong domestic state control.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore licensing pressure
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe is seeking investment for marginal offshore prospects while trying to prevent opaque licensing and unfavorable revenue-sharing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited fiscal capacity leaves ports, energy, and connectivity projects dependent on foreign financiers, increasing exposure to Chinese, Gulf, and European bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract review
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater domestic value capture and transparency in offshore hydrocarbons, creating friction with international operators and prior concession holders.

frictionVectors.title: Financing and debt constraints
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stress and scrutiny of past borrowing limit Dakar's room to fund infrastructure independently, increasing leverage for multilateral lenders, Gulf investors, China, and European partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign basing sensitivities
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles must balance maritime-security cooperation with India, France, and other partners against public concern over sovereignty and any perception of foreign military entrenchment.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on external capital and imported energy leaves critical infrastructure and the tourism economy vulnerable to foreign market, lender, and climate pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore bargaining power
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore operations offer vital export revenue but concentrate infrastructure and fiscal leverage in foreign mining companies, leaving contract terms and local processing politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese project exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, energy, and mining interests expand connectivity but raise concerns about debt sustainability, procurement transparency, and control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore oil competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign exploration interest is increasing, but weak institutions, disputed federal authority, and licensing disagreements risk converting offshore hydrocarbons into a source of internal and external contestation.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and security influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Gulf states, and other partners compete for port, logistics, and security access, complicating Mogadishu's control over strategic infrastructure and maritime policy.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing of platinum-group metals, manganese and other critical minerals while balancing investment from China, Western partners and Gulf states.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, port congestion and weak freight rail continue to reduce state control over export value chains and constrain mining revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on Sudanese export infrastructure, leaving production and state revenue exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption and external commercial leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Armed economic networks
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and localized armed competition continue to divert resource rents and weaken effective government control over oil-producing areas and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized gold networks
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain central to wartime financing, with regional buyers and foreign-linked trading networks capturing value outside effective Sudanese state oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor contest
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, pipelines and key trade routes is strategically contested, exposing national supply chains to armed coercion and external patronage.

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pursuing large-scale gas development while demanding stronger domestic benefits, fiscal terms and local participation from international energy companies.

frictionVectors.title: Port sovereignty debate
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in port and logistics infrastructure has generated concerns over strategic control, although the government continues to use investment agreements to expand trade capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major regional gateway, but reliance on foreign capital, shipping networks and transshipment demand limits the state's control over logistics value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate governance
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains strategically important, yet production and downstream processing face governance, investment and infrastructure constraints that limit national value addition.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and trade access remain tied to migration management and political cooperation, limiting Tunisian room for maneuver. The government is balancing sovereignty claims against dependence on external budget and energy support.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported hydrocarbons and electricity interconnection risks, particularly through reliance on Algeria and European financing for renewable infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Sovereignty and Financing
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and related fields deepen Uganda's dependence on foreign operators, lenders, insurers, and transit arrangements through Tanzania. Environmental, land, and financing disputes continue to challenge Kampala's control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects provide critical capacity but constrain fiscal flexibility through repayment obligations and concentrated contractor dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Western, Chinese, and Gulf-linked investors are competing for copper and cobalt access, creating opportunities for Zambia to demand local processing while risking renewed dependence on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Power Supply Bottleneck
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortages constrain mining expansion and industrial sovereignty. Emergency imports and proposed new generation capacity increase exposure to neighboring grids, private developers, and external financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mineral Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese companies remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and other mining projects, while Zimbabwe seeks beneficiation and export controls without sufficient domestic capital or processing capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Currency Sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions, restricted financial access, and persistent currency instability push Harare toward alternative financing and deeper reliance on non-Western partners. This preserves regime autonomy but raises the cost of infrastructure and resource development.
